abstract: Reciprocal 16p11.2 copy-number variants (CNVs) confer substantial risk for neuropsychiatric disorders and produce opposing effects on brain size, with larger brain volume in deletion carriers and smaller volume in duplication carriers. Regional alterations broadly parallel this global phenotype, but because regional brain measures scale nonlinearly with brain size, it remains unclear whether regional differences reflect expected consequences of altered brain size, regional anatomy disproportionate to brain size, or fundamental alterations in allometric scaling. We analyzed 285 imaging sessions from 235 participants (49 deletion, 59 duplications, 127 controls) using log-log allometric models to distinguish these possibilities. Brain-size adjustment revealed widespread cortical disproportion in both CNVs, with predominantly reciprocal effects driven by surface area rather than cortical thickness, whereas subcortical structures showed convergent reductions disproportionate to brain size. Strikingly, examining genotype-specific scaling exponents revealed distinct allometric patterns between the CNVs. In duplication, regional differences predominantly reflected fixed shifts relative to brain size. In deletion, by contrast, regional differences more frequently varied with brain size, with substantial exponent deviations affecting 32% of disproportionate cortical regions compared with 12% in duplication. Thus, reciprocal 16p11.2 dosage does not simply shift regional anatomy in opposite directions: duplication largely preserves the normally conserved scaling of regional anatomy with brain size, whereas deletion more extensively disrupts it.
